slides.0.title: Principles of fortification and maturation
slides.0.subtitle: When the spirit goes in decides whether the wine is sweet or dry
slides.1.title: Timing of fortification
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Fortifying during fermentation
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Adding grape spirit part-way through fermentation stops the yeast with high alcohol, leaving unfermented sugar → sweet styles (Port, VDN, Rutherglen Muscat)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Fortifying after fermentation
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Ferment to dryness, then add spirit to adjust alcohol → a dry base (most Sherry); sweet Sherries are made by blending in sweet wine afterwards
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Fortifying before fermentation
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Spirit is added to grape juice with almost no fermentation, as in South African Jerepigo, keeping the most grape character and sweetness
slides.1.content: Fortification timing is the sweetness switch: the starting point for every D5 style category.
slides.2.title: Reductive and oxidative maturation
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Reductive
slides.2.highlights.0.content: In large vessels or bottle with little oxygen, preserving fresh fruit and colour (Ruby Port, Vintage Port, young Grenat VDN)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Oxidative
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Long oxygen contact in small casks turns the colour amber and brings nut, caramel and dried-fruit notes (Tawny Port, Oloroso, Madeira, Rivesaltes Tuilé)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Biological (under flor)
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Fino and Manzanilla age under a film of yeast (flor) that shuts out oxygen and consumes glycerol and alcohol, producing acetaldehyde and almond and dough notes; flor survives only at around 15% alcohol
slides.2.content: In blind tasting look at colour and aroma first: red fruit → reductive; amber and nuts → oxidative; salty almond → flor.
slides.3.title: Solera and heated ageing
slides.3.highlights.0.title: The solera system
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Casks are arranged in tiers: wine is drawn for bottling from the oldest tier (solera) and topped up from the next youngest (criadera), and so on up; the result is a consistent multi-vintage blend that cannot carry a vintage
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Heated ageing
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Madeira uses heat to speed oxidation: estufagem heats the wine to about 45–50°C for at least three months, while canteiro ages in casks in warm lofts for years, giving higher quality. Hot sheds in Rutherglen have a similar effect
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Evaporation and concentration
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Long cask ageing evaporates water and alcohol, concentrating acid, sugar and flavour; that is why old Tawny, old Madeira and VORS Sherry often have vivid acidity and intense flavour
slides.3.content: Maturation is the main driver of fortified wine prices: time, casks and evaporation all cost money.
